claim: Research into human genes is heavily skewed towards genes that have been widely studied for decades, including many genes that were being studied before the productive phase of the Human Genome Project.
source: It is known that research into human genes is heavily skewed towards genes that have been widely studied for decades, including many genes that were being studied before the productive phase of the Human Genome Project.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing this pattern in the scientific literature.

claim: The genes most frequently investigated by the research community tend to be only marginally more important to human physiology and disease than a random selection of genes.
source: This means that the genes most frequently investigated by the research community tend to be only marginally more important to human physiology and disease than a random selection of genes.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about gene research patterns and is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The analysis included 10,395 research publications about SARS-CoV-2 that mention at least one human gene.
source: Based on an analysis of 10,395 research publications about SARS-CoV-2 that mention at least one human gene, we report here that the COVID-19 literature up to mid-October 2020 follows a similar pattern.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset analyzed in the study.

claim: The COVID-19 literature up to mid-October 2020 follows a similar pattern to pre-established research patterns.
source: Based on an analysis of 10,395 research publications about SARS-CoV-2 that mention at least one human gene, we report here that the COVID-19 literature up to mid-October 2020 follows a similar pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript comparing COVID-19 literature to non-COVID-19 literature patterns.

claim: A large number of host genes that have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 infection by four genome-wide studies remain unstudied.
source: This means that a large number of host genes that have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 infection by four genome-wide studies remain unstudied.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis showing the proportion of genes identified by genome-wide studies that have not been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.

claim: Researchers identified the host proteins required for viral entry into cells shortly after SARS-CoV-2 emerged as a global threat.
source: Shortly after SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, had emerged as a global threat to human health in January 2020, researchers had identified the host proteins required for viral entry into cells (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Monteil et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Drugs were repurposed for treating COVID-19 patients shortly after SARS-CoV-2 emerged.
source: Shortly after SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, had emerged as a global threat to human health in January 2020, researchers had identified the host proteins required for viral entry into cells (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Monteil et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020), repurposed drugs for treating COVID-19 patients (Grein et al., 2020; Recovery Collaborative Group, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on drug repurposing.

claim: Vaccine development was initiated shortly after SARS-CoV-2 emerged as a global threat.
source: Shortly after SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, had emerged as a global threat to human health in January 2020, researchers had identified the host proteins required for viral entry into cells (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Monteil et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020), repurposed drugs for treating COVID-19 patients (Grein et al., 2020; Recovery Collaborative Group, 2020), and initiated vaccine development (Folegatti et al., 2020; Jackson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on vaccine development.

claim: Early COVID-19 research advances drew upon previous lines of research.
source: A common feature of these advances was that they drew upon previous lines of research.
evidence: This is an inference based on the examples of early COVID-19 research provided in the manuscript.

claim: LitCOVID is a literature hub curated by the National Library of Medicine that tracks publications on COVID-19.
source: To answer this question we used LitCOVID, a literature hub curated by the National Library of Medicine that tracks publications on COVID-19 (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: LitCOVID tags genes within the publicly accessible text of individual publications through PubTator.
source: LitCOVID tags genes within the publicly accessible text of individual publications through PubTator (Wei et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2019.

claim: PubTator applies an ensemble of automated approaches to tag genes and then allows for revision of these tags through biocurators.
source: LitCOVID tags genes within the publicly accessible text of individual publications through PubTator (Wei et al., 2019), which first applies an ensemble of automated approaches to tag genes, and then allows for a revision of these tags through biocurators.
evidence: This describes the methodology of PubTator as cited from Wei et al., 2019.

claim: The analysis yielded 10,395 research publications featuring 3733 human protein-coding genes that have been tagged at least once.
source: This yields 10,395 research publications featuring 3733 human protein-coding genes that have been tagged at least once.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data obtained from the analysis.

claim: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 is the most prominently tagged gene in COVID-19 research.
source: The most prominently tagged genes up to this point are: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2, which serves as receptor for SARS-CoV-2 to enter cells (Hoffmann et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the analysis and a citation explaining the gene's function.

claim: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 serves as receptor for SARS-CoV-2 to enter cells.
source: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2, which serves as receptor for SARS-CoV-2 to enter cells (Hoffmann et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2020.

claim: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 accounts for 10.8% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature.
source: They account for 10.8%, 9.7%, and 4.5% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature, respectively (see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: C-reactive protein is a serum marker for inflammation.
source: C-reactive protein, a serum marker for inflammation (Sproston and Ashworth, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sproston and Ashworth, 2018.

claim: C-reactive protein accounts for 9.7% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature.
source: They account for 10.8%, 9.7%, and 4.5% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature, respectively (see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Interleukin 6 is a mediator of systemic inflammatory responses.
source: Interleukin 6, a mediator of systemic inflammatory responses (Kang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kang et al., 2019.

claim: Interleukin 6 accounts for 4.5% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature.
source: They account for 10.8%, 9.7%, and 4.5% of the total research on human protein-coding genes within the COVID-19 literature, respectively (see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature are enriched for annotations on immune response with a false-discovery rate <10−66.
source: Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis of the human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature finds them enriched for annotations on immune response (false-discovery rate <10−66)
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis performed on the data.

claim: Human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature are enriched for annotations on inflammatory response with a false-discovery rate <10−65.
source: Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis of the human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature finds them enriched for annotations on immune response (false-discovery rate <10−66), inflammatory response (false-discovery rate <10−65)
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis performed on the data.

claim: Human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature are enriched for annotations on defense response to virus with a false-discovery rate <10−31.
source: Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis of the human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature finds them enriched for annotations on immune response (false-discovery rate <10−66), inflammatory response (false-discovery rate <10−65), and defense response to virus (false-discovery rate <10−31) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis performed on the data.

claim: Genome-wide approaches circumvent research patterns that may have been pre-established within the scientific literature.
source: As genome-wide approaches circumvent research patterns that may have been pre-established within the scientific literature (Haynes et al., 2018; Nelson et al., 2015; Stoeger et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: RNA-sequencing was used to identify 1726 host genes that change the expression of their transcripts in the lungs of COVID-19 patients at an adjusted p-value<0.05.
source: RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) was used recently to identify 1726 host genes that change the expression of their transcripts in the lungs of COVID-19 patients at an adjusted p-value<0.05 (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blanco-Melo et al., 2020.

claim: Affinity-purification mass spectrometry was used to identify 293 host proteins following the pulldown of exogenously expressed SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: Affinity-purification mass spectrometry (Aff-MS) was used to identify 293 host proteins following the pulldown of exogenously expressed SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gordon et al., 2020.

claim: The Host Genetics Initiative identified 52 genes through genome-wide association studies at a P-value of 10−5 or lower in one of three comparisons.
source: Using genome-wide association studies (GWAS), the Host Genetics Initiative identified 52 genes through their association at a P-value of 10−5 or lower in one of three comparisons: COVID-19 vs lab or self-reported negative; hospitalized COVID-19 patients vs population; or very severe respiratory COVID-19 vs population (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2020a; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative and Ellinghaus et al., 2020.

claim: 15 genes were identified in two GWAS comparisons.
source: 15 genes were identified in two comparisons and one gene, Leucine zipper transcription factor-like protein 1 (LZTFL1), was identified in all three comparisons (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of GWAS data.

claim: Leucine zipper transcription factor-like protein 1 (LZTFL1) was identified in all three GWAS comparisons.
source: 15 genes were identified in two comparisons and one gene, Leucine zipper transcription factor-like protein 1 (LZTFL1), was identified in all three comparisons (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of GWAS data.

claim: A pooled CRISPR screen was used to identify 41 genes affecting SARS-CoV-2 induced cell death in African green monkey cells.
source: Using a pooled CRISPR screen to affect SARS-CoV-2 induced cell death in African green monkey cells, Wei et al. identified 41 genes, which we mapped to their human homologs using BioMart (Wei et al., 2020; see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2020.

claim: 48 genes are identified in two of the four different genome-wide datasets.
source: 48 genes are identified in two of the four different genome-wide datasets (Supplementary file 3), but no gene is identified in more than two.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of the four genome-wide datasets.

claim: No gene is identified in more than two of the four genome-wide datasets.
source: 48 genes are identified in two of the four different genome-wide datasets (Supplementary file 3), but no gene is identified in more than two.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of the four genome-wide datasets.

claim: 56%–71% of the genes identified in the four genome-wide datasets have not yet been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: However, an analysis of the COVID-19 literature reveals that most (56%–71%) of the genes identified in these four datasets have not yet been tagged in the COVID-19 literature (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and presented in Figure 1A.

claim: 19% of all human protein-coding genes have been tagged at least once in the COVID-19 literature.
source: Thus, the genes identified by the four genome-wide datasets are 10–25% more likely to have been tagged than a randomly chosen gene because we also observe that 19% of all human protein-coding genes have been tagged at least once in the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The genes identified by the four genome-wide datasets are 10–25% more likely to have been tagged than a randomly chosen gene.
source: Thus, the genes identified by the four genome-wide datasets are 10–25% more likely to have been tagged than a randomly chosen gene because we also observe that 19% of all human protein-coding genes have been tagged at least once in the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the tagging rates of genome-wide identified genes to all genes.

claim: The fraction of tagged genes only increases by 0–7% if preprints are included.
source: Similarly, the fraction of tagged genes only increases by 0–7% if we include preprints (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genes identified by multiple genome-wide datasets are more likely to have been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: At the same time, we observe that genes, which have been identified by multiple of the four distinct genome-wide datasets (Figure 1B), or multiple GWAS comparisons (Figure 1C), are more likely to have been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and presented in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Genes identified by multiple GWAS comparisons are more likely to have been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: At the same time, we observe that genes, which have been identified by multiple of the four distinct genome-wide datasets (Figure 1B), or multiple GWAS comparisons (Figure 1C), are more likely to have been tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and presented in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Research into COVID-19 host genes enriches for host genes identified by multiple different lines of support, particularly if there exists support from human genome-wide association studies.
source: This, reassuringly, demonstrates that research into COVID-19 host genes enriches for host genes identified by multiple different lines of support – particularly if there exists support from human genome-wide association studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that genes with multiple lines of evidence are more likely to be tagged.

claim: Genes identified by multiple genome-wide datasets remain only a minority (2%) of all identified genes.
source: Yet, overall, genes identified by multiple genome-wide datasets remain only a minority of all identified genes (2%), and many of them are still ignored in the COVID-19 literature (52%) (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 52% of genes identified by multiple genome-wide datasets are still ignored in the COVID-19 literature.
source: Yet, overall, genes identified by multiple genome-wide datasets remain only a minority of all identified genes (2%), and many of them are still ignored in the COVID-19 literature (52%) (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Knowledge on human genes is heavily skewed toward a subset of genes.
source: Briefly, we know that knowledge on human genes is heavily skewed toward a subset of genes (Gans et al., 2008; Gillis and Pavlidis, 2013; Hoffmann and Valencia, 2003; Oprea et al., 2018; Su and Hogenesch, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five studies.

claim: The most heavily studied genes were being investigated prior to the Human Genome Project.
source: Briefly, we know that knowledge on human genes is heavily skewed toward a subset of genes (Gans et al., 2008; Gillis and Pavlidis, 2013; Hoffmann and Valencia, 2003; Oprea et al., 2018; Su and Hogenesch, 2007) that were being investigated prior to the Human Genome Project (Edwards et al., 2011; Grueneberg et al., 2008; Stoeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: The most frequently investigated protein-coding genes tend to be only marginally more important to human physiology and disease than a random selection of genes when assessed through genetic loss-of-function intolerance or findings of GWAS.
source: As a result, if assessing their importance through genetic loss-of-function intolerance or findings of GWAS (Haynes et al., 2018; Stoeger et al., 2018), the most frequently investigated protein-coding genes tend to be only marginally more important to human physiology and disease than a random selection of genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haynes et al., 2018 and Stoeger et al., 2018.

claim: Genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature are also frequently investigated in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: We find that genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature are also frequently investigated in the non-COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 literature.

claim: The median rank of genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature exceeds the rank of 80% of human protein-coding genes in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: The median rank of genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature exceeds the rank of 80% of human protein-coding genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The majority of protein-coding human genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature was already heavily investigated in the context of research unrelated to COVID-19.
source: This demonstrates that the majority of protein-coding human genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature was already heavily investigated in the context of research unrelated to COVID-19.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that tagged genes have high ranks in non-COVID-19 literature.

claim: For each of the four distinct datasets investigated, ignored genes occur less in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: As anticipated, we observe that for each of the four distinct datasets investigated, ignored genes also occur less in this non-COVID-19 literature (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: For RNA-seq, ignored genes had occurred slightly more in the non-COVID-19 literature (median percentile: 52) with p<10−2.
source: When we compare the number of publications on implicated but ignored host genes to the number of publications on any protein-coding gene encoded in the human genome, this difference is modest, and only reaches statistical significance for RNA-seq (RNA-Seq: p<10−2; Interactomics: p=0.20; GWAS: p=0.93; CRISPR: p=0.31), where ignored genes had occurred slightly more in the non-COVID-19 literature (median percentile: 52).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: For Interactomics, the difference in occurrence of ignored genes in non-COVID-19 literature is not statistically significant (p=0.20).
source: When we compare the number of publications on implicated but ignored host genes to the number of publications on any protein-coding gene encoded in the human genome, this difference is modest, and only reaches statistical significance for RNA-seq (RNA-Seq: p<10−2; Interactomics: p=0.20; GWAS: p=0.93; CRISPR: p=0.31)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: For GWAS, the difference in occurrence of ignored genes in non-COVID-19 literature is not statistically significant (p=0.93).
source: When we compare the number of publications on implicated but ignored host genes to the number of publications on any protein-coding gene encoded in the human genome, this difference is modest, and only reaches statistical significance for RNA-seq (RNA-Seq: p<10−2; Interactomics: p=0.20; GWAS: p=0.93; CRISPR: p=0.31)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: For CRISPR, the difference in occurrence of ignored genes in non-COVID-19 literature is not statistically significant (p=0.31).
source: When we compare the number of publications on implicated but ignored host genes to the number of publications on any protein-coding gene encoded in the human genome, this difference is modest, and only reaches statistical significance for RNA-seq (RNA-Seq: p<10−2; Interactomics: p=0.20; GWAS: p=0.93; CRISPR: p=0.31)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Implicated host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature have occurred significantly more frequently in the non-COVID-19 literature for all four datasets (RNA-Seq: p<10−98; Interactomics: p<10−18; GWAS: p<10−6; CRISPR: p<10−6).
source: In contrast, implicated and tagged host genes have occurred significantly more frequently in the non-COVID-19 literature (RNA-Seq: p<10−98; Interactomics: p<10−18; GWAS: p<10−6; CRISPR: p<10−6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Implicated host genes that are ignored in the COVID-19 literature have in the past been studied as much as randomly chosen human protein-coding genes.
source: We conclude that implicated host genes that are ignored in the COVID-19 literature have in the past been studied as much as randomly chosen human protein-coding genes, whereas implicated host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature have in the past already been investigated much more frequently than randomly chosen human protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of publication frequencies.

claim: Implicated host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature have in the past already been investigated much more frequently than randomly chosen human protein-coding genes.
source: We conclude that implicated host genes that are ignored in the COVID-19 literature have in the past been studied as much as randomly chosen human protein-coding genes, whereas implicated host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature have in the past already been investigated much more frequently than randomly chosen human protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of publication frequencies.

claim: The literature is skewed toward a subset of genes that were being investigated prior to the productive phase of the Human Genome Project.
source: Before the COVID-19 pandemic it had been shown that the literature is skewed toward a subset of genes that were being investigated prior to the productive phase of the Human Genome Project.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge from prior research.

claim: Genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature had occurred earlier in the literature than other genes.
source: We decided to explore if the genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature had been studied before the pandemic, and found that they had occurred earlier (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of gene occurrence presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Many genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature were first studied before the productive phase of the Human Genome Project.
source: We decided to explore if the genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature had been studied before the pandemic, and found that they had occurred earlier (Figure 1E), with many also first being studied before the productive phase of the Human Genome Project (NHGRI, 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of gene occurrence presented in Figure 1E, with reference to NHGRI, 2003.

claim: Host genes identified by the four genome-wide datasets that are ignored in the COVID-19 literature first appeared in the non-COVID-19 literature after the host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: Similarly, the host genes identified by the four genome-wide datasets that are ignored in the COVID-19 literature first appeared in the non-COVID-19 literature after the host genes that are tagged in the COVID-19 literature (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of gene occurrence presented in Figure 1E.

claim: 35% of the genes identified by RNA-seq are among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: The second class holds 35% of the genes identified by RNA-seq, 33% of the genes identified by Aff-MS, 29% of the genes identified by GWAS, and 24% of the genes identified by CRISPR.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 33% of the genes identified by Aff-MS are among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: The second class holds 35% of the genes identified by RNA-seq, 33% of the genes identified by Aff-MS, 29% of the genes identified by GWAS, and 24% of the genes identified by CRISPR.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 29% of the genes identified by GWAS are among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: The second class holds 35% of the genes identified by RNA-seq, 33% of the genes identified by Aff-MS, 29% of the genes identified by GWAS, and 24% of the genes identified by CRISPR.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 24% of the genes identified by CRISPR are among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes in the non-COVID-19 literature.
source: The second class holds 35% of the genes identified by RNA-seq, 33% of the genes identified by Aff-MS, 29% of the genes identified by GWAS, and 24% of the genes identified by CRISPR.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: It will take around one year until nearly all genes among the 50% top-studied human protein-coding genes will have been tagged at least once within the COVID-19 literature.
source: Extrapolating from the observed trends, we anticipate that it will take around one year till nearly all genes of this class will have been tagged at least once within the COVID-19 literature (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a projection based on extrapolation of observed trends in Figure 2A.

claim: For genes among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes, the increase in occurrence in the COVID-19 literature is slower than for the 50% most studied protein-coding genes.
source: When focusing on the genes that are among the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes, we too observe their occurrence in the COVID-19 literature to increase steadily over time (Figure 2B). As for each of the four genome-wide datasets the increase is, however, slower than for the 50% most studied protein-coding genes
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Multiple years could pass until each gene of the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes will have been tagged at least once within the COVID-19 literature.
source: As for each of the four genome-wide datasets the increase is, however, slower than for the 50% most studied protein-coding genes, we project that multiple years could pass until each gene of the 50% least-studied human protein-coding genes will have been tagged at least once within the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This is a projection based on extrapolation of observed trends.

claim: 83% of all human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature have not been identified by any of the four genome-wide datasets.
source: Notably, 83% of all human protein-coding genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature have not been identified by any of the four genome-wide datasets.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The different genome-wide datasets together account for 26% of the COVID-19 literature (RNA-seq: 11.7%, Aff-MS: 2.4%, GWAS: 0.5%, CRISPR: 11.1%).
source: Further, the different genome-wide datasets together only account for 26% of the COVID-19 literature (RNA-seq: 11.7%, Aff-MS: 2.4%, GWAS: 0.5%, CRISPR: 11.1%) (see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The 20% top-tagged human protein-coding genes (747 of 3,733) in the COVID-19 literature account for 90% of the literature.
source: If we consider the current literature, we do indeed observe support for our hypothesis that the COVID-19 literature is becoming dominated by a few genes as currently the 20% top-tagged human protein-coding genes (747 of 3,733) in the COVID-19 literature account for 90% of the literature (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The share of literature accounted for by the 20% top-tagged genes exceeds the 80% anticipated for scientific processes subjected to anthropogenic biases.
source: This share exceeds the 80% anticipated for scientific processes subjected to anthropogenic biases (Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to an expected value from Jia et al., 2019.

claim: A surprisingly small fraction of genes dominates the COVID-19 literature.
source: We conclude that a surprisingly small fraction of genes dominates the COVID-19 literature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that 20% of genes account for 90% of the literature.

claim: The COVID-19 literature has become less expansive over time when measured by the share of literature accounted for by the 20% top-tagged genes.
source: We observe that the COVID-19 has become less expansive, whether we quantify expansiveness through the share of the literature that is accounted for by the 20% top-tagged genes or the Gini coefficient over the share of the COVID-19 literature attributable to individual genes (Gini, 1912; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: The COVID-19 literature has become less expansive over time when measured by the Gini coefficient.
source: We observe that the COVID-19 has become less expansive, whether we quantify expansiveness through the share of the literature that is accounted for by the 20% top-tagged genes or the Gini coefficient over the share of the COVID-19 literature attributable to individual genes (Gini, 1912; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: The COVID-19 literature became more expansive after the first months when assessed by the total number of genes that have been tagged at least once.
source: However, if assessing expansiveness by the total number of genes that have been tagged at least once, then this literature did become more expansive after the first months (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2E.

claim: The share of the COVID-19 literature accounted for by the 100 genes that were tagged first has been decreasing.
source: Interestingly, we also observe that the share of the COVID-19 literature, which is accounted for by the 100 genes that were tagged first within the COVID-19 literature has been decreasing (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: The share of literature accounted for by the first 100 tagged genes has stabilized at roughly 45% since June.
source: Interestingly, we also observe that the share of the COVID-19 literature, which is accounted for by the 100 genes that were tagged first within the COVID-19 literature has been decreasing (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) – though stabilizing at an astonishingly high share of roughly 45% since June (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis presented in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: The literature on COVID-19 became less expansive during the first months of the pandemic and has since stayed focused on a restricted subset of genes.
source: We conclude that, overall, the literature on COVID-19 became less expansive during the first months of the pandemic and has since stayed focused on a restricted subset of genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis of literature expansiveness.

claim: The 100 initially tagged genes are 29% more likely to have been identified by one of the four genome-wide datasets compared to other genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: When contrasting the 100 initially tagged genes against the other genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature, we reassuringly find that the 100 initially tagged genes are 29% more likely to have been identified by one of these four datasets (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis.

claim: The 100 initially tagged genes are on average tagged 2993% more than other genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature.
source: When contrasting the 100 initially tagged genes against the other genes tagged in the COVID-19 literature, we reassuringly find that the 100 initially tagged genes are 29% more likely to have been identified by one of these four datasets (Supplementary file 4). However, they are on average tagged 2993% more (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis.

claim: The 20% top-tagged genes are 3% less likely to have been identified by one of the four genome-wide datasets compared to other tagged genes.
source: If we contrast the 20% top-tagged genes against the other tagged genes, we find them to be 3% less likely to have been identified by one of the four genome-wide datasets, while they on average are tagged 3512% more (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis.

claim: The 20% top-tagged genes are on average tagged 3512% more than other tagged genes.

evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis.

claim: The present focus of the COVID-19 literature on a restricted subset of genes cannot be explained by those genes having been identified by genome-wide datasets.
source: Cumulatively, this suggests that the present focus of the COVID-19 literature on a restricted subset of genes cannot be explained by those genes having been identified by genome-wide datasets reporting on transcriptomic changes, protein interactions, genetic associations and loss-of-function perturbations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis showing that top-tagged genes are not more likely to be identified by genome-wide datasets.

claim: It cannot be determined whether a gene tagged in the COVID-19 literature is truly investigated for its potential role in COVID-19.

source: Second, we cannot yet assess how important individual genes are in COVID-19.

claim: There is a significant risk that the COVID-19 literature will continue to ignore host genes that have not already been extensively studied independently of COVID-19.

claim: Research into human protein-coding genes is disproportionately skewed towards a comparably small set of genes.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three prior studies.

claim: Genes identified by genome-wide datasets that had not already been investigated more than other genes prior to COVID-19 have remained ignored in the COVID-19 literature.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis in the study.

claim: There is an exploration-exploitation trade-off at play in COVID-19 research.

evidence: This is an inference about the dynamics of scientific research.

claim: Focusing research on genes that have already been heavily investigated yields significant advantages including applicability of existing research tools, the ability to place findings in a broader context, and the identification of drugs and other reagents that could be repurposed.
source: We realize that there is an exploration-exploitation trade-off at play and that focusing research on genes that have already been heavily investigated yields significant advantages to investigators: applicability of existing research tools, the ability to place findings in a broader context, and the identification of drugs and other reagents that could be repurposed.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical advantages of studying well-characterized genes.

claim: Interventions in clinical trials on COVID-19 are biased toward pharmaceutical targets that occurred frequently in the non-COVID-19 literature.

claim: Antibodies are less available for genes identified by RNA-seq or Aff-MS or GWAS which have been ignored in the COVID-19 literature.
